avô.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *avōlus (variant of Classical aviolus, diminutive of avus 'grandfather'), with closed stressed [o] contrasting with feminine avó (< *aviola).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: avô

azeite.etymology: From Arabic az-zayt ('juice of the olive, olive oil'), where the definite article al- assimilated to the following z-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: azeite

azeite.notes: In Brazilian Portuguese, azeite used alone refers specifically to olive oil, while óleo covers seed and mechanical oils.

azul.etymology: Transmitted via Andalusi Arabic and Medieval Latin from Classical Arabic lāzaward ('lapis lazuli'), from Persian lāžward ('lapis lazuli'); the initial l- was dropped by reanalysis as the Romance/Arabic definite article.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: azul

azul-escuro.etymology: Compound color adjective formed in Portuguese from azul ('blue' < Arabic lāzaward < Persian lāžward) + escuro ('dark' < Latin obscūrus).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: azul-escuro

aço.etymology: Derived via Old Portuguese from Late Latin aciārium / *aciō ('steeled edge'), rooted in Classical Latin aciēs ('sharp edge, blade point').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: aço

aço.notes: Essential for high-tension piano strings (cordas de aço) and hand tools.

açúcar.etymology: Entered Portuguese via Andalusi Arabic as-sukkar, from Persian šakar, ultimately from Sanskrit śarkarā ('gravel, grit, candied sugar crystals').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: açúcar

açúcar.notes: Retained the assimilated Arabic definite article a(s)-, unlike French sucre or English sugar.

aí.etymology: Formed in Old Portuguese from the preposition a (< Latin ad) + í / hi ('there' < Latin ibī, blended with hīc), denoting a place near the listener or 'then'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: aí

badalada.etymology: Derived from badalo ('bell clapper' < Late Latin batāculum / Vulgar Latin *battuāculum, instrument noun from Latin battuere 'to beat, strike') + -ada ('stroke of a bell').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: badalada

bagagem.etymology: Borrowed from French bagage ('luggage, travelling equipment'), derived from Old French bague ('bundle, pack, sack').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: bagagem

bairro.etymology: From Andalusi Arabic bárri ('outer, suburban'), derived from Classical Arabic barr ('open land outside town walls').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: bairro

bairro.notes: Standard word throughout Brazil and Portugal for a local residential neighbourhood.

baixar.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *bassiāre ('to lower, make low'), derived from Late Latin bassus ('thickset, low').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: baixar

baixinho.etymology: Diminutive of baixo ('low, short, quiet' < Late Latin bassus) formed with the suffix -inho (< Latin -īnus), frequently used adverbially to mean 'softly, in a low voice'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: baixinho

baixo.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bassius, a palatalized derivative of Late Latin bassus ('thick, short, low in height').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: baixo

balconista.etymology: Formed in Portuguese from balcão ('shop counter' < Italian balcone) + occupational suffix -ista, naming a clerk who serves customers at a counter.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: balconista

balcão.etymology: Borrowed from Italian balcone ('balcony, large window sill, shop counter'), an augmentative derived from Lombardic/Germanic *balko ('wooden beam, timber').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: balcão

balde.etymology: Shared with Spanish balde ('bucket, pail'); its ultimate origin in this sense is uncertain in Priberam and Iberian etymological dictionaries, distinct from the homophonous adverb em balde ('in vain' < Arabic bāṭil).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: balde

bambo.etymology: Expressive formation meaning 'loose, slack, wobbly', built on an onomatopoetic root *bamb- imitating swaying or unsteady motion (compare Italian bambo and Ancient Greek bambaínō 'to totter').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: bambo

banca.etymology: Feminine variant of banco ('bench, table, market stall, newsstand, examining board'), borrowed via Romance from Germanic *bankiz ('bench, shelf').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: banca

bandeira.etymology: Derived from banda ('ensign, banner, troop' < Gothic bandwō 'sign, standard' or Frankish *binda 'strip, band') + suffix -eira.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: bandeira

bandeja.etymology: From Old Portuguese bandejar ('to winnow grain by tossing it from side to side on a flat vessel'), derived from banda ('side').

history.meaning: side -> to rock or winnow from side to side

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: bandeja

banheiro.etymology: Inherited from Latin balneārium ('bathhouse, bathroom') or formed directly from banho ('bath' < Latin balneum) + suffix -eiro (< -ārium).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: banheiro

banho.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *banjum, from Classical Latin balneum / balineum ('bath'), borrowed from Ancient Greek balaneîon ('bathing-place').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: banho

banquinho.etymology: Diminutive of banco ('bench, stool' < Germanic *bankiz) formed with the Portuguese diminutive suffix -inho.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: banquinho

barro.etymology: Priberam records barro as a pre-Roman Hispanic substrate word (*barro, 'mud, clay') shared across Portuguese and Spanish.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: barro

barro.notes: Names both wet earth and potter's clay used for earthenware cups, jugs, and flowerpots.

barulhento.etymology: Derived in Portuguese from barulho ('noise, clatter, commotion') + adjectival suffix -ento ('full of, prone to').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: barulhento

barulho.etymology: Origin uncertain; Priberam notes it is an expressive Iberian word for 'commotion, noise, hubbub', variously linked to a Vulgar Latin derivative of volvere ('to roll, churn') or an onomatopoetic root *bar-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: barulho

base.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin basis ('pedestal, foundation'), from Ancient Greek básis ('step, foot, base, pedestal'), derived from baínō ('to step, walk').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: base

bastante.etymology: Originally the present participle of bastar ('to suffice, be enough' < Vulgar Latin *bastāre 'to support, suffice'), used as an adjective ('sufficient') and adverb ('quite, plenty').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: bastante

bater.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *battere, a popular reduction of Classical Latin battuere ('to beat, strike, pound'), itself a borrowing from Gaulish.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: bater

batida.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle of bater ('to beat, strike, knock, shake' < Latin battuere), naming a knock, beat, crash, or shaken fruit cocktail.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: batida

baú.etymology: Borrowed via Spanish baúl or Old French bahut ('domed travelling trunk, chest'), a medieval European word of uncertain ultimate origin.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: baú

beco.etymology: Origin uncertain; Priberam records beco ('narrow alley, dead-end lane') without a settled etymon, though scholars have proposed Celtic beccus ('beak, narrow point') or pre-Roman substrate origins.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: beco

belo.etymology: From Latin bellus ('pretty, handsome, fine'), originally a diminutive (*duenelos) of Old Latin duenos (> Classical bonus 'good'), reinforced in Portuguese by Italian and Provençal literary influence (preserving single -l-).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: belo

bem.etymology: Inherited from Latin bene ('well, rightly'), the adverb corresponding to bonus ('good'), with apocope of -e and nasalization of the stressed vowel.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: bem

bem-vindo.etymology: Compound adjective formed in Portuguese from bem ('well' < Latin bene) + vindo ('come, arrived', past participle of vir < Latin venīre).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: bem-vindo

biblioteca.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin bibliothēca, from Ancient Greek bibliothḗkē ('book repository, library', compounded from biblíon 'book' + thḗkē 'case, repository').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: biblioteca

bico.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin beccus ('bird's beak, bill'), attested in Suetonius as a word of Gaulish (Celtic) origin; extended metaphorically to spouts, tips, and odd jobs.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: bico

bilhete.etymology: Borrowed from French billet ('short written note, ticket'), diminutive of Old French bille / bulle ('sealed note, document' < Medieval Latin bulla 'seal, official document').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: bilhete

bisbilhotar.etymology: Derived in Portuguese from bisbilhoteiro ('gossipy, nosy'), likely borrowed or adapted from Italian bisbigliare ('to whisper, murmur furtively'), of expressive onomatopoetic origin (bis-bis).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: bisbilhotar

biscoito.etymology: From Medieval Latin biscoctus (pānis) (or via Old French bescuit), literally 'twice-baked (bread)', from Latin bis ('twice') + coctus ('cooked, baked', past participle of coquere).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: biscoito

bloquear.etymology: Borrowed from French bloquer ('to blockade, obstruct, lock'), derived from Middle French bloc ('solid log, block, obstacle' < Middle Dutch blok).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: bloquear

blusa.etymology: Borrowed from French blouse ('loose workman's smock, blouse'), a word first recorded in 18th-century French whose deeper origin remains uncertain.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: blusa

bolha.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bullia or diminutive bullula, from Classical Latin bulla ('water bubble, blister, round boss').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: bolha

bolo.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin bōlus ('lump, morsel, mass' < Ancient Greek bôlos 'clod, lump'), which specialized in Portuguese for a round baked mass of sweet dough ('cake').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: bolo

bolsinha.etymology: Diminutive of bolsa ('purse, handbag, pouch' < Late Latin bursa < Ancient Greek býrsa 'dressed hide, leather bag') formed with the suffix -inha.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: bolsinha

bolso.etymology: Masculine back-formation from bolsa ('bag, purse' < Late Latin bursa < Ancient Greek býrsa 'hide, leather sack'), specialized in Portuguese to denote a sewn-in garment pocket.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: bolso

bom.etymology: Inherited from Latin bonus ('good'), via Old Portuguese bõo with regular loss of intervocalic -n- and nasalization of the vowel.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: bom

bonito.etymology: Formed in Iberian Romance as a diminutive of bono ('good' < Latin bonus) + -ito, evolving semantically from 'nice, dainty' to 'pretty, handsome'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: bonito

bora.etymology: An informal shortening of embora, used to encourage someone to go or do something. Priberam treats this separately from the unrelated name of an Adriatic wind, which comes from Italian. The office invitation uses the Portuguese encouragement.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: bora

borda.etymology: Borrowed via Romance from Frankish/Germanic *bord ('edge, rim, ship's side, plank').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: borda

botão.etymology: Borrowed from Old French boton (modern bouton, 'flower bud, knob, button'), derived from Old French boter ('to push out, sprout, thrust' < Frankish *bōtan 'to strike, push').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: botão

branco.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *blancus, borrowed from Proto-Germanic *blankaz ('shining, bright, white'), with regular Portuguese rhotacism of initial bl- to br-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: branco

bravo.etymology: Shared across Western Romance (bravo 'wild, fierce, courageous, angry'); most widely derived from Vulgar Latin *brabus, a popular dissimilation of Classical Latin barbarus ('untamed, foreign, fierce').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: bravo

braço.etymology: Priberam derives braço from Latin bracchium ('forearm, arm'), itself from Greek brakhíōn.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: braço

braço.notes: Used literally for the human arm and by extension for chair armrests or extra helpers ('mais dois braços').

briga.etymology: Shared with Italian briga ('strife, quarrel, trouble') and Old Occitan briga, traced to a Late Latin/Celtic root *brīga ('strength, valor, contention').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: briga

brigar.etymology: Derived from the noun briga ('quarrel, fight' < Celtic/Late Latin *brīga 'contention, strife') + verbal suffix -ar.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: brigar

brilhante.etymology: Present participial adjective of brilhar ('to shine, sparkle' < Italian brillare).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: brilhante

brilhar.etymology: Borrowed from Italian brillare ('to sparkle, glitter like a cut gem'), generally traced to Latin bēryllus ('beryl crystal' < Ancient Greek bḗryllos).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: brilhar

brinde.etymology: Borrowed via Spanish brindis or Italian brindisi ('drinking toast, complimentary gift'), from the 16th-century German phrase bring dir's! ('I bring it to you! / I toast you!').

history.meaning: I bring it (the cup) to you

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: brinde

bule.etymology: Borrowed during 16th-century Portuguese maritime trade in Maritime Southeast Asia from Malay buli-buli ('small gourd, flask, spouted vessel').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: bule

bule.notes: Travelled along the same Asian sea routes that brought chá ('tea') into Portuguese.

buscar.etymology: Shared with Spanish buscar ('to seek, look for, fetch'), from Old Portuguese boscar, a word of uncertain pre-Roman (Celto-Iberian) origin.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: buscar

caber.etymology: Inherited from Latin capere ('to take, hold, contain, have capacity for'), which shifted in Iberian Romance to 'to fit inside, be contained', with voicing of intervocalic -p- to -b-.

history.meaning: to take, hold, have room for

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: caber

cabeça.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *capitia ('head'), derived from Classical Latin caput, capitis ('head').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cabeça

cada.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin cata ('each, every'), borrowed from Ancient Greek katá ('down, by, apiece, distributively', as in katà mía 'one by one').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cada

cadeira.etymology: Inherited from Latin cathedra ('armchair, teacher's seat'), borrowed from Ancient Greek kathédra ('seat, chair', from katá 'down' + hédra 'seat'), with regular Galician-Portuguese development of -dr- > -ir-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cadeira

caderno.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin quaternum ('quire of four folded sheets, notebook'), from Classical Latin quaternī ('four each'), derived from quattuor ('four').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: caderno

cadê.etymology: Colloquial Brazilian Portuguese phonetic reduction of the interrogative phrase que é de...? ('what has become of...? / where is...?'), via intermediate forms quedê and cadê.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cadê

cafeteira.etymology: Formed from café ('coffee') + instrument suffix -teira, modeled on French cafetière ('coffee pot, coffee maker').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cafeteira

café.etymology: Borrowed via French café and Italian caffè from Ottoman Turkish kahve, itself from Arabic qahwah ('coffee, originally a dark brew or wine').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: café

cair.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cadēre / *cadīre (for Classical Latin cadere 'to fall'), with regular Galician-Portuguese loss of intervocalic -d-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cair

caixa.etymology: Borrowed via Old Occitan or Catalan caissa / caixa from Latin capsa ('box, case, repository for scrolls'), related to capere ('to hold, contain').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: caixa

cajueiro.etymology: Formed within Brazilian Portuguese from caju ('cashew') + the tree suffix -eiro (< Latin -ārium); caju comes from Old Tupi aka'yu ('cashew fruit').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cajueiro

cajueiro.notes: Iconic shade and fruit tree of Northeastern Brazilian courtyards, including Recife.

calado.etymology: Participial adjective of calar ('to fall silent, stop speaking'), from Late Latin chalāre ('to lower sails, slacken, subside' < Ancient Greek khaláō 'to loosen, slacken').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: calado

calcanhar.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *calcāneāre, derived from Classical Latin calcāneum ('heel'), itself from calx, calcis ('heel of the foot').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: calcanhar

calcanhar.notes: Related to the verb calcar ('to tread, press down with the foot').

calda.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin calda (syncopated feminine of Classical Latin calida [aqua], 'hot liquid, warm bath'), from calidus ('warm, hot'), specialized for melted sugar syrup.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: calda

calma.etymology: Transmitted via Late Latin cauma ('burning heat of the midday sun, when wind and work cease'), from Ancient Greek kaûma ('heat', from kaíō 'to burn'), shifting to 'windless stillness, tranquility'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: calma

calmo.etymology: Derived from the noun calma ('stillness, tranquility' < Late Latin cauma < Ancient Greek kaûma 'midday heat when the wind dies down').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: calmo

calor.etymology: Calor continues Latin calor, -oris ('warmth, heat'), related to calere ('to be warm').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: calor

calor.notes: Masculine noun (o calor); fazer calor describes warm weather and estar com calor describes feeling warm.

calçada.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle of calçar ('to pave with stones, shoe' < Vulgar Latin *calciāre, from Latin calceus 'shoe' / calx 'heel or limestone'), naming a paved street or sidewalk.

history.meaning: to shoe, pave with tamped stones

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: calçada

calçar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *calciāre (Classical Latin calceāre, 'to put on shoes, furnish with footwear'), derived from calceus ('shoe'), from calx, calcis ('heel').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: calçar

cama.etymology: Inherited from Hispano-Latin cama ('low bed near the ground', attested in Isidore of Seville), a word of pre-Roman Paleohispanic substrate origin.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cama

caminhada.etymology: From the verb caminhar (to walk) + -ada (suffix for action or duration).

caminho.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin camminus ('way, road, path'), borrowed from Gaulish (Celtic) *kammīnos ('path, way', related to *kamb- / *kamm- 'step').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: caminho

caminhão.etymology: Adapted from French camion ('heavy dray, freight truck'), reshaped in Brazilian Portuguese by folk-etymological association with caminho ('road') + augmentative -ão (European Portuguese camião).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: caminhão

camisa.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin camisia ('linen shirt or tunic'), a Celtic (Gaulish) loanword into Roman Latin.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: camisa

camomila.etymology: From Late Latin chamomilla, borrowed from Greek khamaímēlon ('earth-apple'), compounded from khamaí ('on the ground') + mêlon ('apple') after the apple-like fragrance of its blossoms.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: camomila

camomila.notes: Chá de camomila is one of Brazil's best-loved calming evening infusions.

campainha.etymology: Diminutive of Old Portuguese campãa ('bell' < Late Latin campāna, originally 'Campanian bronze vessel/bell') + diminutive suffix -inha.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: campainha

caneca.etymology: Derived from cana ('reed, cylindrical vessel' < Latin canna) or borrowed via maritime trade from Middle Dutch/Low German kanneke ('small tankard, mug', diminutive of kanne 'jug').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: caneca

canela.etymology: From Vulgar Latin cannella ('small reed, little tube'), diminutive of Classical Latin canna ('reed, cane'), applied both to rolled cinnamon quills and to the long tubular shinbone.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: canela

caneta.etymology: Borrowed from Italian cannetta or French canette ('small reed tube, penholder'), diminutive of canna ('reed, hollow tube' < Latin canna).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: caneta

cano.etymology: Formed as a masculine noun from Latin canna ('reed, cane, hollow pipe' < Ancient Greek kánna), specialized in Portuguese for a water pipe, tube, or gun barrel.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cano

cantar.etymology: Inherited from Latin cantāre ('to sing, chant'), the frequentative of canere ('to sing').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cantar

canto.etymology: Converges two Latin etyma: in the sense 'corner, angle, edge', from Latin canthus ('iron rim of a wheel, corner' < Ancient Greek kanthós or Celtic *kantos); in the sense 'singing, song', from Latin cantus (from canere 'to sing').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: canto

caprichado.etymology: Participial adjective of caprichar ('to take great care, do with flair and thoroughness'), derived from capricho (< Italian capriccio 'whim, lively artistic fancy').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: caprichado

cara.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin cara ('face, countenance'), borrowed from Ancient Greek kárā ('head, face').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cara

cardápio.etymology: Coined in 1889 in Rio de Janeiro by Brazilian philologist Antônio de Castro Lopes from Latin charta ('sheet, paper') + daps, dapis ('feast, meal, dish') as a vernacular substitute for French menu.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cardápio

cardápio.notes: One of the rare deliberate neologisms that caught on completely, becoming the standard everyday word for 'menu' across Brazil.

cargo.etymology: Deverbal noun from Old Portuguese cargar / carregar ('to load, entrust with an office' < Late Latin carricāre 'to load a wagon', from Gaulish-Latin carrus).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cargo

carimbo.etymology: Borrowed from Kimbundu ka'rimbu ('branding iron used to mark cattle or captives, stamp'), formed from the diminutive prefix ka- + rimbu ('mark, brand').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: carimbo

caro.etymology: Inherited from Latin cārus ('dear, beloved, costly, high-priced').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: caro

carregar.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin carricāre ('to load onto a wagon, transport'), derived from Latin carrus ('four-wheeled wagon', of Gaulish origin).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: carregar

carro.etymology: Inherited from Latin carrus ('four-wheeled baggage wagon'), borrowed from Gaulish (Celtic) *karros ('wagon, chariot').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: carro

carta.etymology: Inherited from Latin charta ('leaf of papyrus, sheet of paper, epistle, charter'), borrowed from Ancient Greek khártēs ('sheet of papyrus').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: carta

carteiro.etymology: Derived in Portuguese from carta ('letter' < Latin charta) + occupational suffix -eiro (< Latin -ārius).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: carteiro

cartão.etymology: Borrowed from Italian cartone (or French carton, 'heavy pasteboard, card'), augmentative of carta ('sheet of paper' < Latin charta).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cartão

cartão-postal.etymology: Compound noun formed from cartão ('card' < Italian cartone) + postal ('relating to the mail service' < French postal, from Italian posta).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cartão-postal

casa.etymology: Inherited from Latin casa ('hut, cottage, cabin'), which replaced Classical domus in Vulgar Latin as the universal word for 'house, home'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: casa

casaco.etymology: Masculine adaptation of French casaque or Italian casacca ('long riding coat, outer jacket'), a 16th-century European garment word of uncertain ultimate origin.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: casaco

casal.etymology: Inherited from Medieval Latin casāle ('rural homestead, farmstead worked by a household'), derived from Latin casa ('house'), shifting to 'married couple, pair'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: casal

casaquinho.etymology: Diminutive of casaco ('coat, cardigan, jacket') formed with the Portuguese diminutive suffix -inho.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: casaquinho

casca.etymology: Deverbal noun from cascar ('to peel, crack shells or bark'), from Vulgar Latin *quassicāre ('to shake repeatedly, crack, shatter'), frequentative of Classical Latin quassāre.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: casca

casquinha.etymology: Diminutive of casca ('peel, bark, thin crisp shell') formed with -inha, used in Brazilian Portuguese for a crisp wafer ice-cream cone or a thin crust.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: casquinha

catorze.etymology: Inherited from Latin quattuordecim ('fourteen'), a compound of quattuor ('four') and decem ('ten').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: catorze

causa.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin causa ('cause, reason, motive, lawsuit'), forming a learned doublet alongside the inherited popular word coisa ('thing').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: causa

caçula.etymology: Borrowed in Brazilian Portuguese from Kimbundu kasule ('youngest child in a family'), derived from the verb kusula ('to remain at the bottom, be the last').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: caçula

cedo.etymology: Inherited from Latin citō ('quickly, soon, early'), adverb of citus ('swift', from ciēre 'to set in motion'), with regular voicing of intervocalic -t- to -d-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cedo

cedro.etymology: Descends from Latin cedrus ('cedar tree, cedarwood'), borrowed from Ancient Greek kédros ('cedar, juniper').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cedro

cem.etymology: Inherited from Latin centum ('one hundred'), via apocope of Old Portuguese cento when standing proclitically before a noun.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cem

cenoura.etymology: From older Portuguese acenoura (after reinterpreting initial a- as the feminine article), borrowed from Andalusi Arabic safunnárya, ultimately from Greek staphylînē ('carrot, parsnip').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cenoura
Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cento

central.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin centrālis ('situated in the middle, central'), derived from centrum ('center' < Ancient Greek kéntron).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: central

centro.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin centrum ('stationary point of a compass, midpoint'), from Ancient Greek kéntron ('sharp point, pivot leg of a compass').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: centro

centímetro.etymology: Borrowed from French centimètre, coined in the metric system from Latin centum ('hundred', combining form centi- 'one hundredth') + Ancient Greek métron ('measure').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: centímetro

certeza.etymology: Derived in Romance from certo ('certain, sure' < Latin certus) + abstract noun suffix -eza (< Latin -itia).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: certeza

certinho.etymology: Diminutive of certo ('right, exact, sure' < Latin certus) formed with the suffix -inho, used colloquially for 'just right, spot on, neatly'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: certinho

certo.etymology: Inherited from Latin certus ('determined, settled, sure, certain'), originally a participial formation of cernere ('to sift, discern, decide').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: certo

cerâmica.etymology: Priberam derives cerâmica from Greek keramikḗ ('pottery art'), built on kéramos ('potter's clay').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cerâmica

cerâmica.notes: Carries a circumflex accent on â before nasal m in Brazilian spelling (cerâmica).

cesta.etymology: Priberam traces cesta to Latin cista ('wicker box, basket'), from Greek kístē.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cesta

cesta.notes: Standard word for a handled market or picnic basket (cesta de feira).

chafariz.etymology: From Andalusi Arabic šahríǧ / ṣahríǧ, from Classical Arabic ṣihrīj ('water basin, cistern, public fountain'), borrowed from Middle Persian čāh-rēg.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: chafariz

chamar.etymology: Inherited from Latin clāmāre ('to cry out, call upon, summon, name'), with regular Galician-Portuguese palatalization of initial cl- to ch-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: chamar

chato.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *plattus ('flat, level'), borrowed from Ancient Greek platýs ('broad, flat'), with regular Galician-Portuguese shift of initial pl- to ch-; extended figuratively to 'dull, tedious, annoying'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: chato

chave.etymology: Chave descends directly from Latin clāvem (nominative clāvis, 'key'), illustrating the hallmark Galician-Portuguese palatalization of Latin initial cl- to ch-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: chave

chave.notes: Used for door keys, wrenches/spanners (chave de fenda, chave de afinar), and musical clefs (clave, the learned doublet).

chefe.etymology: Priberam gives French chef as the source. The French word goes back to Latin caput, head, so a chefe is the person at the head of a group. In the guesthouse Jorge uses it as a teasing title for the owner; the cooking sense, chef, is a later specialised use.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: chefe

chegar.etymology: Inherited from Latin plicāre ('to fold'), which in nautical Vulgar Latin meant 'to furl sails upon reaching land', hence 'to arrive' (cognate with Spanish llegar), with initial pl- > ch-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: chegar

cheio.etymology: Inherited from Latin plēnus ('full, filled'), with regular Galician-Portuguese palatalization of initial pl- to ch- and loss of intervocalic -n- (plēnu > cheo > cheio).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cheio

cheiro.etymology: Deverbal noun from cheirar ('to smell, emit an odor'), inherited from Latin frāgrāre ('to emit a scent') via dissimilated Vulgar Latin *flāgrāre, with regular initial fl- > ch-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cheiro

cheiro-verde.etymology: Compound noun formed in Brazilian Portuguese from cheiro ('fragrance, aromatic herb') + verde ('green' < Latin viridis), naming the fresh culinary herb bundle of parsley and green onions.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cheiro-verde

chorar.etymology: Inherited from Latin plōrāre ('to wail, lament, weep'), with regular Galician-Portuguese palatalization of initial pl- to ch-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: chorar

chover.etymology: Descends from Vulgar Latin *plovĕre (reshaping Classical Latin pluĕre, 'to rain'), with regular Galician-Portuguese palatalization of initial pl- > ch-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: chover

chover.notes: Compare the parallel shift in cheio (< plēnus) and chamar (< clāmāre).

chuva.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *plōvia (for Classical Latin plŭvia, 'rain', from pluĕre 'to rain'), with regular Galician-Portuguese shift of initial pl- to ch- (plōvia > chuvia > chuva).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: chuva

chuva.notes: Learned adjectives pluvial and chuvoso represent the erudite and inherited branches of the same root.

chuveiro.etymology: Derived in Portuguese from chuva ('rain' < Vulgar Latin plovia, Classical pluvia, with pl- > ch-) + instrument suffix -eiro (< Latin -ārium).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: chuveiro

chá.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century via Portuguese trade in Macao from Cantonese càa (茶, 'tea', Middle Chinese ɖˠa).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: chá

chá.notes: Portuguese traders introduced the Cantonese cha form directly to Europe (while Dutch traders carried Hokkien tê, giving English tea and French thé).

chão.etymology: Inherited from Latin plānus ('flat, level'), via initial pl- > ch- and nasalization/loss of intervocalic -n- (*chão < chano < plānum).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: chão

chão.notes: Forms an inherited/learned doublet with plano ('flat; floor plan').

cidade.etymology: Inherited from Latin cīvitās, cīvitātis ('citizenship, community of citizens, city'), derived from cīvis ('citizen'), via Old Portuguese cibdade / cidade.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cidade

cima.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin cyma ('young sprout, topmost shoot, crest, summit'), borrowed from Ancient Greek kŷma ('swelling, wave, sprout').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cima

cinco.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin cīnque ('five'), formed by dissimilation of the initial labiovelar from Classical Latin quīnque.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cinco

cinquenta.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin cīnquāgintā ('fifty'), dissimilated from Classical Latin quīnquāgintā.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cinquenta

cinza.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cinīsia ('ashes'), derived from Classical Latin cinis, cineris ('ash, embers'); used both for 'ash' and the color 'ash-gray'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cinza

cinza-escuro.etymology: Compound color adjective formed in Portuguese from cinza ('ash-gray' < Vulgar Latin *cinīsia) + escuro ('dark' < Latin obscūrus).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cinza-escuro

claro.etymology: Semi-learned descendant of Latin clārus ('bright, shining, clear, distinct, famous').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: claro

cliente.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin cliēns, clientis ('dependent under a patron's protection, client'), related to clīnāre ('to lean on') or cluēre ('to hear, heed').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cliente

clique.etymology: Onomatopoetic borrowing from French clic (and reinforced in computing by English click), imitating the sharp snap of a latch, switch, or button.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: clique

cobre.etymology: Cobre continues Late Latin cuprum, shortened from aes Cyprium ('metal of Cyprus').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cobre

cobre.notes: Homophonous in speech with 3rd-person singular cobre from cobrir ('covers'), distinguished cleanly by context (fio de cobre).

coisa.etymology: Inherited from Latin causa ('cause, reason, legal matter, affair'), which broadened in Vulgar Latin to mean 'matter, object, thing' (via Old Portuguese cousa > coisa).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: coisa

cola.etymology: In the sense 'glue, paste', inherited via Vulgar Latin colla from Ancient Greek kólla ('glue').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cola

colher.etymology: From Latin cochleāre ('spoon'), derived from cochlea ('snail shell', < Greek kokhlías) because small pointed spoons were used to eat snails and eggs.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: colher

colher.notes: Spelled identically to the verb colher ('to gather, pick', < Latin colligĕre), though the noun has an open stressed vowel [koˈʎɛʁ / koˈʎeʁ].

colocar.etymology: Borrowed from Latin collocāre ('to put in place, station, arrange'), compounded from com- ('together') + locāre ('to place', from locus 'place').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: colocar

coluna.etymology: Priberam derives coluna from Latin columna ('pillar, upright support'), with regular assimilation of Latin -mn- to -n- in Portuguese.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: coluna

coluna.notes: Refers both to architectural pillars and vertical columns in a ledger or newspaper.

com.etymology: Inherited from Latin cum ('with, together with').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: com

combinado.etymology: Participial adjective and agreement interjection ('agreed! / deal!') of combinar, from Late Latin combīnāre ('to join two by two', from com- + bīnī 'two at a time').

history.meaning: to join two by two, combine

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: combinado

comemorar.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin commemorāre ('to call to mind, recount, celebrate in memory'), from com- + memorāre (from memor 'mindful').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: comemorar

comer.etymology: Inherited from Latin comedere ('to eat up, consume completely', from com- + edere 'to eat'), with regular Galician-Portuguese loss of intervocalic -d-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: comer

comercial.etymology: Derived from comércio ('commerce, trade' < Latin commercium, from com- + merx, mercis 'merchandise') + adjectival suffix -al.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: comercial

começar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cominitiāre ('to begin, initiate'), compounded from com- + initiāre ('to begin, originate', from initium 'beginning').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: começar

começo.etymology: Deverbal noun from começar ('to begin, start' < Vulgar Latin *cominitiāre, from Latin initium 'beginning').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: começo

comigo.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cum mēcum, a pleonastic reinforcement of Classical Latin mēcum ('with me', from mē + enclitic cum), with voicing of intervocalic -c- to -g-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: comigo

como.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *quōmo, reduced from Classical Latin quōmodo ('in what manner, how, as', from ablative quō 'by which' + modō 'manner, measure').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: como

compasso.etymology: Deverbal noun from compassar, continuing Vulgar Latin *compassāre ('to measure out in equal steps'), from com- + passus ('pace, step').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: compasso

compasso.notes: Names both a musical bar/measure and a pair of drawing compasses.

completamente.etymology: Formed in Portuguese from the feminine adjective completa ('complete, full' < Latin complētus) + adverbial suffix -mente (< Latin ablative mente 'with a ... mind').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: completamente

completo.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin complētus ('filled up, full, finished'), past participle of complēre ('to fill up, complete', from com- + plēre 'to fill').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: completo

compositora.etymology: Feminine of compositor, learned borrowing from Latin compositor, compositōris ('one who puts together, arranger, author'), from compōnere ('to put together, compose').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: compositora

comprador.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin comparātor, comparātōris ('purchaser, buyer') or formed directly from comprar ('to buy' < Latin comparāre) + agentive suffix -dor.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: comprador

comprar.etymology: Inherited from Latin comparāre ('to get ready, procure, furnish, purchase', from com- + parāre 'to prepare'), with syncope of the pretonic vowel.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: comprar

comprimento.etymology: Derived in Old Portuguese from comprir / cumprir ('to fulfill, reach full extent' < Latin complēre 'to fill up') + -mento; differentiated orthographically with -o- for 'length' versus cumprimento ('greeting, fulfillment').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: comprimento

computador.etymology: Derived from computar ('to calculate, reckon' < Latin computāre, from com- + putāre 'to reckon') + -dor, and semantically shaped by English computer.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: computador

concerto.etymology: Borrowed from Italian concerto ('agreement, musical ensemble or performance'), deverbal from concertare (< Late Latin concertāre 'to contend, bring into harmony').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: concerto

conferir.etymology: Borrowed from Latin conferre ('to bring together, compare, check side by side, bestow'), compounded from com- ('together') + ferre ('to bear, bring').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: conferir

confessar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *confessāre, built on confessus, the past participle of Classical Latin confitērī ('to acknowledge, admit fully', from com- + fatērī 'to admit').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: confessar

confirmar.etymology: From Latin confirmāre ('to make firm, strengthen, establish, verify'), from com- + firmāre ('to make firm', from firmus 'steadfast, firm').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: confirmar

confiável.etymology: Derived from confiar ('to trust, confide' < Vulgar Latin *confīdāre, for Classical confīdere 'to trust fully', from com- + fīdere 'to trust') + suffix -ável (< Latin -ābilis).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: confiável

confortável.etymology: Derived from confortar ('to strengthen, comfort, console' < Late Latin confortāre, from com- + fortis 'strong') + suffix -ável, semantically shaped in its modern sense ('providing physical ease') by French confortable and English comfortable.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: confortável

confusão.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin confūsiō, confūsiōnis ('a mingling together, disorder, confusion'), from confundere ('to pour together, mix up', from com- + fundere 'to pour').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: confusão

conhecer.etymology: Inherited from Latin cognōscere ('to become acquainted with, learn, know'), compounded from com- + (g)nōscere ('to come to know').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: conhecer

conosco.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cum nōscum, a pleonastic reinforcement of Classical Latin nōbīscum ('with us', remodeled on accusative nōs + cum), with reduction of geminate -nn- in Brazilian Portuguese (European Portuguese connosco).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: conosco

conseguir.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *consequīre, an active remodeling of Classical Latin deponent consequī ('to follow closely, overtake, attain, achieve', from com- + sequī 'to follow').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: conseguir

consertar.etymology: From Latin consertāre (frequentative of conserere 'to join together, fit, mend, put in order', from com- + serere 'to link, entwine'), differentiated in modern Portuguese spelling with -s- ('to repair') from concertar.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: consertar

conserto.etymology: Deverbal noun from consertar ('to repair, mend, put in order' < Latin consertāre, from conserere 'to join together').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: conserto

consigo.etymology: As a pronoun ('with oneself / with you'), inherited from Vulgar Latin *cum sēcum, a pleonastic reinforcement of Classical Latin sēcum ('with oneself'); also the first-person singular present indicative of conseguir.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: consigo

conta.etymology: Deverbal noun from contar ('to count, reckon' < Latin computāre), naming a calculation, bill, bank account, or prayer bead used for counting.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: conta

contagem.etymology: Derived in Portuguese from contar ('to count' < Latin computāre) + suffix -agem (< Latin -āticum via Gallo-Romance).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: contagem

contar.etymology: Inherited from Latin computāre ('to sum up, reckon, calculate', from com- + putāre 'to trim, reckon, consider'), with syncope of the pretonic vowel; extended in Romance to 'to recount, tell a story'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: contar

continuar.etymology: Borrowed from Latin continuāre ('to join without a break, make continuous, carry on'), derived from continuus ('uninterrupted', from continēre 'to hold together').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: continuar

contra.etymology: Inherited directly from Latin contrā ('against, opposite, facing').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: contra

contratar.etymology: Derived from contrato ('contract, agreement' < Latin contractus) + verbal suffix -ar.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: contratar

contrato.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin contractus ('a drawing together, bargain, legal agreement'), derived from contrahere ('to draw together, conclude a deal', from com- + trahere 'to draw').

history.meaning: to draw together, enter into an agreement

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: contrato

conversa.etymology: Deverbal noun from conversar ('to talk together, converse' < Latin conversārī).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: conversa

conversar.etymology: From Latin conversārī ('to live with, keep company with, associate with', from com- + versāre 'to turn about frequently'), which shifted in Romance from 'keeping company' to 'talking together'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: conversar

conversão.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin conversiō, conversiōnis ('a turning around, transformation, conversion'), action noun of convertere ('to turn around, change', from com- + vertere 'to turn').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: conversão

copo.etymology: Inherited from Late/Vulgar Latin cuppus, a masculine variant of Classical Latin cuppa ('tub, cask, drinking cup').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: copo

cor.etymology: From Old Portuguese coor, inherited from Latin color, colōris ('colour, hue') via regular loss of intervocalic -l- and contraction of the resulting hiatus.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cor

cor.notes: Feminine in Portuguese (a cor), unlike masculine Spanish el color.

corajoso.etymology: Derived from coragem ('courage' < Old Occitan coratge / Old French corage < Vulgar Latin *corāticum, from Latin cor 'heart') + adjectival suffix -oso (< Latin -ōsus).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: corajoso

coração.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *corāciōne, an expressive enlargement formed from Classical Latin cor, cordis ('heart').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: coração

corda.etymology: From Latin chorda ('musical string, cord, catgut'), borrowed from Greek khordḗ.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: corda

corda.notes: Unlike Spanish cuerda, Portuguese kept Latin short ŏ undiphthongized as open [ɔ].

corpo.etymology: Inherited from Latin corpus, corporis ('body, physical frame, substance').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: corpo

corredor.etymology: Derived from correr ('to run' < Latin currere) + suffix -dor (< Latin -tōrem / -tōrium), denoting both a 'runner' and a 'long narrow passageway' (reinforced by Italian corridore).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: corredor

correr.etymology: Inherited directly from Latin currere ('to run, hasten, flow').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: correr

correria.etymology: Derived in Portuguese from correr ('to run' < Latin currere) + suffix -eria, naming a bustle, rush, or hurried running about.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: correria

corrida.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle of correr ('to run' < Latin currere), denoting a run, race, or taxi ride.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: corrida

cortar.etymology: Inherited from Latin curtāre ('to shorten, clip, cut off'), derived from the adjective curtus ('shortened, cut short').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cortar

cortina.etymology: From Late Latin cortīna ('curtain, hanging drapery', in the Vulgate for the hangings of the Tabernacle), associated with cohors / cortis ('enclosed court').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cortina

costumar.etymology: Derived from costume ('custom, habit' < Vulgar Latin *cōnsuētūmen, for Classical cōnsuētūdō, cōnsuētūdinis 'habit, custom', from cōnsuēscere 'to grow accustomed') + -ar.

history.meaning: to be accustomed to, usually do

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: costumar

couro.etymology: Inherited from Latin corium ('thick hide, skin, leather'), via regular metathesis of the palatal glide (coriu > coiro > couro).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: couro

cozinha.etymology: Continues Late Latin cocīna (Classical coquīna, 'kitchen, cooking art'), derived from coquĕre ('to cook').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cozinha

cozinha.notes: Base of cozinhar ('to cook') and cozinheiro ('cook, chef').

coçar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *coctiāre ('to feel a burning itch, scratch'), derived from coctus ('cooked, smarting, burning', past participle of coquere).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: coçar

creme.etymology: Borrowed from French crème ('cream'), from Old French cresme, a phonetic convergence of Late Latin chrisma ('anointing oil' < Ancient Greek khrîsma) and Gaulish-Latin crama ('milk cream').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: creme

crescer.etymology: Inherited from Latin crēscere ('to come into being, grow, increase, thrive').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: crescer

crocante.etymology: Adapted from French croquant ('crunchy, crisp'), present participle of croquer ('to crunch between the teeth'), of onomatopoetic origin.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: crocante

cubinho.etymology: Diminutive of cubo ('cube' < Latin cubus < Ancient Greek kýbos 'six-sided die, cube') formed with the Portuguese suffix -inho.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cubinho

cuidado.etymology: Inherited from Latin cōgitātus ('thought, reflection'), past participle of cōgitāre (> cuidar 'to think, attend to, care for'), used as a noun ('care, caution') and warning interjection.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cuidado

cuidar.etymology: Inherited from Latin cōgitāre ('to think, ponder, reflect upon', from com- + agitāre), via Old Portuguese coidar > cuidar, shifting semantically from 'giving thought to' to 'taking care of'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: cuidar

culpa.etymology: Learned or semi-learned descendant of Latin culpa ('fault, blame, offense, guilt').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: culpa

curioso.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin cūriōsus ('full of care, diligent, inquisitive, eager to know'), derived from cūra ('care, attention').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: curioso

curto.etymology: Inherited from Latin curtus ('shortened, clipped, brief, short').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: curto

curva.etymology: Substantivized feminine of the Latin adjective curvus, curva ('bent, curved, bowed').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: curva

custar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin costāre, from Classical Latin cōnstāre ('to stand firm, stand at a price, cost', from com- + stāre 'to stand').

history.meaning: to stand together, cost a price

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: custar

céu.etymology: Inherited from Latin caelum ('sky, heaven, vault of the heavens'), with regular Galician-Portuguese loss of intervocalic -l- (caelu > ceo > céu).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: céu

danado.etymology: Inherited from Latin damnātus ('condemned, damaged, ruined'), past participle of damnāre (from damnum 'loss, damage'); used colloquially in Brazil for 'mischievous, clever, extreme'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: danado

daquele.etymology: Contraction formed in Portuguese from the preposition de ('of, from' < Latin dē) + the demonstrative aquele ('that' < Vulgar Latin *eccu(m) ille).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: daquele

daqui.etymology: Contraction formed in Portuguese from the preposition de ('from, of' < Latin dē) + the adverb aqui ('here' < Vulgar Latin *eccu(m) hīc).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: daqui

dar.etymology: Inherited directly from Latin dare ('to give, grant, offer').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: dar

data.etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin data ('given [on such a day]'), the feminine singular or neuter plural past participle of dare ('to give') used in the dating clause of epistles and charters.

history.meaning: to give / given (date of a document)

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: data

de.etymology: The preposition continues Latin de. It can express origin, membership or a relation between things. In de marketing it names the meeting’s subject; do combines de with the masculine article o in the employee’s department phrase.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: de

debaixo.etymology: Formed in Portuguese from the preposition de ('from, at' < Latin dē) + baixo ('low, lower part' < Late Latin bassus).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: debaixo

decibel.etymology: International acoustics term coined from Latin decimus ('tenth', combining form deci-) + bel (unit named after telephone pioneer Alexander Graham Bell).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: decibel

decisão.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin dēcīsiō, dēcīsiōnis ('a cutting off, settlement, decision'), derived from dēcīdere ('to cut off, determine', from dē- + caedere 'to cut').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: decisão

dedo.etymology: Dedo descends from Latin digitus ('finger, toe') via syncope of the unstressed vowel and voicing of intervocalic -t- to -d-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: dedo

dedo.notes: Learned doublet dígito is used for numerical digits.

degrau.etymology: From Old Portuguese degrau, formed from de- + grau ('step, degree' < Latin gradus 'step, pace, stair', reinforced by Late Latin dēgradus).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: degrau

deixar.etymology: From Old Portuguese leixar, inherited from Latin laxāre ('to loosen, slacken, let go, release', from laxus 'loose'), with replacement of initial l- by d- (likely through crossing with delaxāre or dar).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: deixar

deixe-me.etymology: Verb-clitic phrase formed in Portuguese from deixe (present subjunctive / formal imperative of deixar 'to let, allow' < Latin laxāre) + enclitic first-person object pronoun me (< Latin mē).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: deixe-me

dela.etymology: Contraction formed in Galician-Portuguese from the preposition de ('of, from' < Latin dē) + third-person feminine pronoun ela ('she, her' < Latin illa).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: dela

dele.etymology: Contraction formed in Galician-Portuguese from the preposition de ('of, from' < Latin dē) + third-person masculine pronoun ele ('he, him' < Latin ille).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: dele

delicioso.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin dēliciōsus ('delightful, delicious'), derived from Classical Latin dēliciae ('delight, pleasure, luxury').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: delicioso

demais.etymology: Formed in Portuguese by fusing the preposition de (< Latin dē) + mais ('more' < Latin magis), meaning 'in excess, too, besides'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: demais

demorar.etymology: From Latin dēmorārī ('to linger, tarry, delay, dwell'), compounded from dē- + morārī ('to delay, stay', from mora 'delay, pause').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: demorar

dentro.etymology: Inherited from Latin dē intrō ('from within, inside'), fusing the preposition dē with the adverb intrō ('inward, within').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: dentro

depender.etymology: Borrowed from Latin dēpendēre ('to hang down from, be suspended from, depend on'), compounded from dē- ('down from') + pendēre ('to hang').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: depender

depois.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dē postius (or dē post, 'afterward, behind'), combining Latin dē ('from') + post / postius ('after, behind').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: depois

depressa.etymology: Formed in Portuguese by fusing the prepositional phrase de pressa ('in haste, quickly'), where pressa ('haste, urgency') comes from Late Latin pressa (from premere 'to press').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: depressa

derramar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dērāmāre ('to strip branches, scatter branches, disperse, spill out'), formed from dē- + rāmus ('tree branch').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: derramar

desabar.etymology: Formed in Portuguese from privative des- (< Latin dis-) + aba ('overhanging edge, brim, eaves, slope') + -ar, literally 'to give way at the edge, collapse, cave in'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: desabar

desanimar.etymology: Formed from privative prefix des- (< Latin dis-) + animar ('to give spirit/life to' < Latin animāre, from anima 'breath, spirit').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: desanimar

desastre.etymology: Borrowed via French désastre from Italian disastro ('ill-starred event, calamity'), formed from pejorative dis- + astro ('star, planet' < Latin astrum < Ancient Greek ástron).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: desastre

descansar.etymology: Formed in Iberian Romance from reversive des- (< Latin dis-) + cansar ('to tire, weary' < Latin campsāre 'to double a headland, turn from a course' < Ancient Greek kámptō 'to bend').

history.meaning: to turn aside, grow weary from a voyage

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: descansar

descanso.etymology: Deverbal noun from descansar ('to rest, take a break' < des- + cansar).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: descanso

descer.etymology: Inherited from Latin dēscendere ('to climb down, come down, descend', from dē- + scandere 'to climb'), via dissimilated Old Portuguese decer.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: descer

descobrir.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin discoperīre ('to uncover, lay bare, disclose'), the reversive of cooperīre ('to cover completely').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: descobrir

desconhecido.etymology: Participial adjective and noun from desconhecer ('not to know, be unacquainted with'), formed from negative des- + conhecer (< Latin cognōscere 'to know').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: desconhecido

desconto.etymology: Deverbal noun from descontar ('to deduct from an account, discount' < des- + contar < Latin computāre, reinforced by Italian sconto).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: desconto

desculpa.etymology: Deverbal noun from desculpar ('to clear of blame, excuse, forgive' < des- + culpa 'fault, blame').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: desculpa

desculpar.etymology: Formed in Romance from privative des- (< Latin dis-) + culpar ('to blame', from Latin culpa 'fault, guilt'), meaning 'to free from blame, excuse, pardon'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: desculpar

desde.etymology: Formed in Old Portuguese by combining des ('from, since' < Vulgar Latin *dē ex) + the preposition de (< Latin dē).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: desde

desejar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dēsīdiāre ('to long for, desire'), derived from Classical Latin dēsīdium ('longing, desire', alongside dēsīderāre).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: desejar

desenhado.etymology: Participial adjective of desenhar ('to draw, sketch, design' < Italian disegnare < Latin dēsignāre).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: desenhado

desenhar.etymology: Borrowed from Renaissance Italian disegnare ('to draw, trace, design'), itself from Latin dēsignāre ('to mark out, trace, designate', from dē- + signum 'mark, sign').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: desenhar

desenho.etymology: Deverbal noun from desenhar, modeled on Italian disegno ('drawing, sketch, design' < Latin dēsignāre).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: desenho

desligar.etymology: Formed from reversive prefix des- (< Latin dis-) + ligar ('to bind, connect, turn on' < Latin ligāre 'to tie, bind'), meaning 'to unbind, disconnect, turn off'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: desligar

deslizar.etymology: Shared with Spanish deslizar ('to slide, glide, slip'), formed from des- + a stem related to liso ('smooth, sleek, slippery') + -izar.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: deslizar

despensa.etymology: Inherited from Medieval Latin dispēnsa ('pantry, storehouse where household provisions are weighed and distributed'), feminine past participle of Latin dispendere ('to weigh out, dispense').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: despensa

despertador.etymology: Derived in Portuguese from despertar ('to wake up, rouse' < Vulgar Latin *dēexpertāre, built on Latin expertus 'awakened, active') + instrument/agent suffix -dor.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: despertador

dessa.etymology: Contraction formed in Portuguese from the preposition de ('of, from' < Latin dē) + the feminine medial demonstrative essa ('that' < Latin ipsa).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: dessa

desse.etymology: Contraction formed in Portuguese from the preposition de ('of, from' < Latin dē) + the masculine medial demonstrative esse ('that' < Latin ipse).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: desse

deste.etymology: Contraction formed in Portuguese from the preposition de ('of, from' < Latin dē) + the masculine proximal demonstrative este ('this' < Latin iste).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: deste

destrancar.etymology: Formed in Portuguese from reversive des- (< Latin dis-) + trancar ('to bar, bolt, lock', from tranca 'wooden crossbar, door bolt', of pre-Roman Celtic *tranka 'beam, pole' origin).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: destrancar

detestar.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin dētestārī ('to curse while calling the gods as witnesses, execrate, loathe'), from dē- + testārī ('to bear witness', from testis 'witness').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: detestar

deus.etymology: Inherited (with ecclesiastical retention of final -s) from Latin deus ('god, deity').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: deus

devagar.etymology: Formed in Old Portuguese by fusing the prepositional phrase de vagar ('at leisure, unhurriedly, slowly'), where vagar descends from Latin vacāre ('to be empty, have free time').

history.meaning: to be empty, be at leisure

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: devagar

dever.etymology: Inherited from Latin dēbēre ('to owe, be under obligation, ought to'), contracted in early Latin from dē- + habēre ('to have from another').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: dever

devolver.etymology: Borrowed from Latin dēvolvere ('to roll down, unroll; in Romance, to hand back, return'), compounded from dē- + volvere ('to roll, turn').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: devolver

dez.etymology: Inherited from Latin decem ('ten'), with regular assibilation of palatalized -c- and loss of the final syllable.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: dez

dezenove.etymology: Analogical compound formed in Romance from dez ('ten' < Latin decem) + e ('and' < Latin et) + nove ('nine' < Latin novem), replacing Classical Latin ūndēvīgintī.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: dezenove

dezesseis.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *decem et sex ('ten and six', replacing Classical Latin sēdecim 'sixteen'), compounded from dez + e + seis.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: dezesseis

dia.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dia, a first-declension remodeling of Classical Latin diēs ('day').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: dia

dignidade.etymology: Semi-learned descendant of Latin dignitās, dignitātis ('worthiness, merit, honorable standing, dignity'), derived from dignus ('worthy').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: dignidade

dinheiro.etymology: Inherited from Latin dēnārius ('Roman silver coin originally worth ten asses', from dēnī 'by tens', from decem 'ten'), which became the general Portuguese noun for 'money'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: dinheiro

direita.etymology: Substantivized feminine of direito ('straight, right' < Vulgar Latin *dērēctus), elliptically from mão direita ('right hand, right-hand side').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: direita

direitinho.etymology: Diminutive of direito ('straight, right, proper' < Vulgar Latin *dērēctus) formed with the suffix -inho, used to mean 'neatly, properly, just right'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: direitinho

direito.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dērēctus (for Classical Latin dīrēctus, 'straight, upright, direct, just'), past participle of dīrigere ('to set straight, guide').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: direito

direto.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin dīrēctus ('straight, direct, without detour'), forming a learned doublet of the inherited popular form direito.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: direto

discrição.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin discrētiō, discrētiōnis ('distinction, discernment, prudence, tact'), derived from Classical Latin discernere ('to separate, discern').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: discrição

discurso.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin discursus ('a running about; in Late Latin, conversation, treatise, formal speech'), from discurrere ('to run about, speak at length').

history.meaning: to run to and fro, discourse

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: discurso

disputar.etymology: Borrowed from Latin disputāre ('to weigh, examine, argue, debate, contend for'), compounded from dis- + putāre ('to reckon, consider').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: disputar

disso.etymology: Contraction formed in Portuguese from the preposition de ('of, from, about' < Latin dē) + the neuter medial demonstrative pronoun isso ('that' < Latin ipsum).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: disso

distância.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin distantia ('standing apart, remoteness, interval, distance'), derived from distāre ('to stand apart', from dis- + stāre 'to stand').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: distância

dividir.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin dīvidere ('to force apart, separate, distribute, divide').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: dividir

dizer.etymology: Inherited from Latin dīcere ('to say, speak, tell, state').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: dizer

dobradiça.etymology: Derived in Portuguese from dobrado ('folded', past participle of dobrar < Latin duplāre) + suffix -iça (< Latin -īcia), naming a metal hinge that folds open and shut.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: dobradiça

dobrado.etymology: Inherited from Latin duplātus ('doubled, folded in two'), past participle of duplāre (> dobrar 'to double, fold').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: dobrado

dobrar.etymology: Inherited from Latin duplāre ('to double, fold in two'), derived from duplus ('double, twofold'), with regular voicing of -p- to -b- and shift of post-consonantal -l- to -r-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: dobrar

dobro.etymology: Inherited from Latin duplum ('twice as much, the double'), neuter substantive of duplus ('double, twofold').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: dobro

dobrável.etymology: Derived in Portuguese from dobrar ('to fold' < Latin duplāre) + adjectival suffix -ável (< Latin -ābilis), meaning 'foldable, collapsible'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: dobrável

doce.etymology: Inherited from Latin dulcis, dulce ('sweet, pleasant'), via vocalization of preconsonantal -l- (dulce > douce > doce).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: doce

documento.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin documentum ('lesson, example, proof, official record'), derived from docēre ('to teach, show').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: documento

dois.etymology: Inherited from Latin duōs, masculine accusative plural of duo ('two'), via Old Portuguese dous > dois.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: dois

domingo.etymology: From Late Latin [diēs] Dominĭcus ('the Lord's day'), derived from dominus ('lord').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: domingo

domingo.notes: Unlike Portuguese Monday–Friday (segunda-feira through sexta-feira), domingo and sábado kept their ancient names.

dona.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin domna, syncopated form of Classical Latin domina ('mistress of a household, lady, owner'), feminine of dominus.

history.meaning: mistress of the house, lady, owner

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: dona

dono.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin domnus, syncopated form of Classical Latin dominus ('master of a household, lord, owner'), derived from domus ('house').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: dono

dor.etymology: Inherited from Latin dolor, dolōris ('pain, ache, grief', from dolēre 'to feel pain'), with regular Galician-Portuguese loss of intervocalic -l- (dolōre > door > dor).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: dor

dormir.etymology: Inherited directly from Latin dormīre ('to sleep').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: dormir

dourado.etymology: Inherited from Latin deaurātus ('gilded, golden'), past participle of deaurāre ('to overlay with gold', from dē- + aurum 'gold').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: dourado

doze.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dōdece, reduced from Classical Latin duodecim ('twelve', from duo 'two' + decem 'ten').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: doze

dueto.etymology: Borrowed from Italian duetto ('musical composition for two performers'), diminutive derived from due ('two' < Latin duo).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: dueto

durante.etymology: From the Latin present participle dūrāns, dūrantis (used in ablative absolute constructions such as vītā dūrante 'while life lasts'), from dūrāre ('to last, endure').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: durante

duro.etymology: Inherited directly from Latin dūrus ('hard, firm, solid, tough').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: duro

década.etymology: Learned borrowing via Late Latin decas, decadīs from Ancient Greek dekás, dekádos ('group of ten, ten-year period'), derived from déka ('ten').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: década

dó.etymology: Converges two origins: in the sense 'pity, compassion, sorrow' (via Old Portuguese doo), from Latin dolus ('grief, pain', related to dolēre 'to ache, grieve'); as the first note of the musical scale, borrowed from Italian do.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: dó

dúzia.etymology: Priberam traces dúzia (via Old French douzaine or Romance *duodena reshaped on doze) ultimately to Latin duodecim ('twelve').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: dúzia

dúzia.notes: Meia dúzia ('half a dozen') is an idiomatic everyday Brazilian way to say 'six' or 'a few'.

e.etymology: Inherited from Latin et ('and'), with regular loss of final -t.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: e

eco.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin ēchō, from Ancient Greek ēkhṓ ('reflected sound, echo'), related to ēkhḗ ('sound, ringing').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: eco

educado.etymology: From Latin ēducātus, past participle of ēducāre ('to bring up, rear, train'), used in Portuguese both for 'educated' and 'polite, well-mannered'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: educado

ela.etymology: Inherited from Latin illa ('that woman, she'), feminine nominative/ablative singular of the distal demonstrative ille.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ela

ele.etymology: Inherited from Latin ille ('that man, he'), masculine singular of the distal demonstrative pronoun.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ele

elegante.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin ēlegāns, ēlegantis ('choosy, tasteful, refined, graceful'), derived from the stem of ēligere ('to choose carefully').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: elegante

eles.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *illēs (remodeled plural of Classical Latin ille / illōs, 'those men, they').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: eles

em.etymology: Inherited from Latin in ('in, into, on'), via Old Portuguese en with regular labialization of final nasal.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: em

embaixo.etymology: Formed in Portuguese by fusing the prepositional phrase em baixo ('in the low part, underneath'), from em (< Latin in) + baixo (< Late Latin bassus).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: embaixo

embora.etymology: Contraction of the Old Portuguese phrase em boa hora ('in a good hour, auspiciously' < Latin in bonā hōrā), originally a wish for a safe departure (ir-se embora) and later grammaticalized as the concessive conjunction 'although'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: embora

embrulhado.etymology: Participial adjective of embrulhar ('to wrap up, bundle, muddle'), related to Italian imbrogliare and French embrouiller (from a Romance stem *brodiculāre 'to mix, tangle, bundle').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: embrulhado

emergência.etymology: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ēmergentia ('an arising, unforeseen event requiring urgent action'), from Classical Latin ēmergere ('to rise out of water, surface').

history.meaning: to rise up, come to the surface

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: emergência

empurrar.etymology: Shared with Old Spanish empurrar ('to shove, push hard'), formed from em- (< Latin in-) + an expressive Iberian root *purr- denoting a forceful thrust (or altered from Latin impulsāre).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: empurrar

encaixar.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed in Portuguese from em- (< Latin in-) + caixa ('box, case, mortise, groove' < Latin capsa) + -ar, meaning 'to fit snugly into a slot or box'.

history.meaning: to fit into a socket, slot in

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: encaixar

encarar.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed in Portuguese from em- (< Latin in-) + cara ('face' < Vulgar Latin cara < Ancient Greek kárā) + -ar, meaning 'to look squarely in the face, confront'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: encarar

encher.etymology: Inherited from Latin implēre ('to fill up, make full', from in- + plēre 'to fill'), with regular Galician-Portuguese palatalization of internal -mpl- to -nch-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: encher
