encontrar.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin incontrāre ('to meet face to face, come upon'), formed from the Latin phrase in contrā ('opposite, facing').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: encontrar

encontro.etymology: Deverbal noun from encontrar ('to meet, come across' < Late Latin incontrāre, from in contrā 'facing, opposite').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: encontro

encostar.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed in Romance from em- (< Latin in-) + costa ('rib, side, back, slope' < Latin costa 'rib, side') + -ar, meaning 'to lean one's side or back against, place alongside'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: encostar

endereço.etymology: Deverbal noun from endereçar ('to direct straight, guide, address a letter' < Vulgar Latin *indīrēctiāre, from in- + dīrēctus 'straight, direct').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: endereço

enganar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ingannāre ('to mock, trick, deceive'), related to Late Latin gannāre ('to jeer, mock') and Classical Latin gannīre ('to yelp, snarl').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: enganar

engano.etymology: Deverbal noun from enganar ('to deceive, mislead; reflexively, to be mistaken' < Vulgar Latin *ingannāre).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: engano

engraçado.etymology: Participial adjective of engraçar ('to endow with charm or wit', from em- + graça 'grace, charm, humor' < Latin grātia), meaning 'funny, amusing, cute'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: engraçado

enorme.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin ēnormis ('out of rule, irregular, immense, vast'), compounded from ex- ('out of') + norma ('carpenter's square, rule, standard').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: enorme

enquanto.etymology: Formed in Old Portuguese by fusing the phrase em quanto ('in how much [time], while, whereas' < Latin in quantō).

history.meaning: in how much, for as long as

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: enquanto

enrolar.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed from em- (< Latin in-) + rolo ('roll, coil, cylinder' < Latin rotulus, diminutive of rota 'wheel') + -ar.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: enrolar

ensaiar.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin exagiāre ('to weigh, test, try out'), derived from exagium ('a weighing, balance, trial' < Classical exigere), with replacement of initial ex- by en-.

history.meaning: weighing, trial / to test, try out

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ensaiar

ensolarado.etymology: Parasynthetic adjective formed in Portuguese from em- + solar ('of the sun', from sol < Latin sōl) + -ado, meaning 'bathed in sunshine, sunny'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ensolarado

entrar.etymology: Inherited from Latin intrāre ('to go inside, enter'), derived from the adverb/preposition intrā ('inside, within').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: entrar

entrega.etymology: Deverbal noun from entregar ('to hand over, deliver' < Latin integrāre).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: entrega

entregar.etymology: Inherited from Latin integrāre ('to make whole, restore intact', from integer 'whole, untouched'), with metathesis of -r-; shifted in Iberian Romance from 'restoring a pledge intact' to 'handing over, delivering'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: entregar

então.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *intunce ('then, at that time'), an enlarged compound based on Classical Latin tunc ('then'), via Old Portuguese enton / entom.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: então

envelope.etymology: Borrowed from French enveloppe ('folded paper cover for a letter'), deverbal noun from envelopper ('to wrap up, enclose').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: envelope

equipe.etymology: Borrowed from French équipe ('work crew, team'), back-formed from équiper ('to outfit a ship or crew' < Old French esquiper, from Old Norse skipa 'to fit out a ship, man a vessel', from skip 'ship').

history.meaning: ship / to man a ship, outfit

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: equipe

erguido.etymology: Participial adjective of erguer ('to raise, lift up, set upright'), which descends from Vulgar Latin *ergere, syncopated from Classical Latin ērigere ('to raise up, erect').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: erguido

errado.etymology: Inherited from Latin errātus, past participle of errāre ('to wander, stray from the right path, make a mistake').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: errado

errar.etymology: Inherited directly from Latin errāre ('to wander aimlessly, go astray, miss the mark, make an error').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: errar

erro.etymology: Deverbal noun from errar ('to stray, make a mistake' < Latin errāre, alongside Classical Latin error).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: erro

erva.etymology: Inherited from Latin herba ('grass, green shoot, culinary or medicinal herb'), with regular spirantization of post-liquid -b- to -v-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: erva

escada.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *scalāta ('flight of steps, ladder'), derived from Classical Latin scāla ('ladder, stairs', from scandere 'to climb'), with regular Galician-Portuguese loss of intervocalic -l-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: escada

escala.etymology: Semi-learned descendant (or borrowing via Italian scala) of Latin scāla ('ladder, stair, graduated scale, port of call'), derived from scandere ('to climb').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: escala

escola.etymology: Descends from Latin schola ('leisure devoted to learning, lecture, school'), borrowed from Ancient Greek skholḗ ('leisure, learned discussion, school').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: escola

escolha.etymology: Deverbal noun from escolher ('to choose, select' < Vulgar Latin *excolligere).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: escolha

escolher.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excolligere ('to pick out from a group, select, choose'), compounded from ex- ('out of') + Classical Latin colligere ('to gather, collect').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: escolher

esconder.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excondere, remodeled with prefix ex- from Classical Latin abscondere ('to put out of sight, hide away', from abs- + condere 'to store away').

history.meaning: to put out of sight, hide

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: esconder

escondido.etymology: Participial adjective of esconder ('to hide, conceal' < Vulgar Latin *excondere < Classical Latin abscondere).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: escondido

escorregar.etymology: Shared with Galician and Spanish escorregar ('to slip, slide'); most often traced to a Vulgar Latin intensive verb *excurricāre (built on currere 'to run, slide') or a pre-Roman substrate formation.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: escorregar

escrever.etymology: Inherited from Latin scrībere ('to trace, draw lines, write'), with prosthetic e- before the initial sC- cluster and spirantization of intervocalic -b- to -v-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: escrever

escrito.etymology: Inherited from Latin scrīptus ('written'), past participle of scrībere ('to write').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: escrito

escritório.etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin scrīptōrium ('writing room, study, office'), derived from the supine stem of Latin scrībere ('to write').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: escritório

esculpir.etymology: Semi-learned descendant of Latin sculpere ('to carve, chisel, sculpt in stone or wood'), with prosthetic e- before initial sc-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: esculpir

escuro.etymology: Inherited from Latin obscūrus ('dark, dim, shadowy'), via Vulgar Latin reduction of the initial cluster (*scūrus > escuro).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: escuro

escutar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin ascultāre (dissimilated from Classical Latin auscultāre 'to listen attentively, lend an ear'), with prefix substitution to es-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: escutar

esfriar.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed in Portuguese from es- (< Latin ex-) + frio ('cold' < Latin frīgidus) + -ar, meaning 'to grow cold, cool down'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: esfriar

espalhar.etymology: Formed in Romance from es- (< Latin ex-) + palha ('straw, chaff' < Latin palea) + -ar (compare Vulgar Latin *expandiculāre), originally meaning 'to scatter straw or chaff', hence 'to spread out, scatter'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: espalhar

espaço.etymology: Espaço continues Latin spatium ('room, distance, interval of space or time'), with prosthetic e- before initial s + consonant.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: espaço

espaço.notes: Ocupar espaço means 'to take up room'.

especial.etymology: Semi-learned descendant of Latin speciālis ('individual, particular, special'), derived from speciēs ('appearance, kind, sort', from specere 'to look at').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: especial

espelho.etymology: Inherited from Latin speculum ('mirror, looking-glass'), an instrument noun derived from specere ('to look, behold'), with regular palatalization of -c'l- to -lh-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: espelho

esperar.etymology: Inherited from Latin spērāre ('to hope for, look forward to, expect'), which expanded semantically in Iberian Romance to include 'to wait for'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: esperar

espiar.etymology: Borrowed via Romance from Frankish/Germanic *spehōn ('to look closely, watch, scout, spy on'), prefixed with es- (< Latin ex-).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: espiar

esponja.etymology: From Latin spongia ('sponge'), borrowed from Greek spongiá, with regular prosthetic e- before initial sp-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: esponja

esponja.notes: Used for natural sea sponges and household cleaning sponges alike.

esquecer.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excadescere ('to fall out of the mind, slip from memory'), formed from ex- ('out of') + cadere ('to fall') + inchoative suffix -ēscere.

history.meaning: to drop out of memory, forget

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: esquecer

esquentar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *excalentāre ('to make warm, heat up'), built on calēns, calentis, the present participle of Classical Latin calēre ('to be warm, hot').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: esquentar

esquerda.etymology: Substantivized feminine of esquerdo ('left'), elliptically from mão esquerda ('left hand, left-hand side').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: esquerda

esquerdo.etymology: Shared across Iberian Romance (Spanish izquierdo, Catalan esquerre); borrowed from a pre-Roman Vasconic/Pyrenean substrate closely related to Basque ezker ('left').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: esquerdo

esquina.etymology: Borrowed via Western Romance from Germanic *skina ('shinbone, narrow strip, sharp ridge or angle'), naming the outward-projecting angle where two walls or streets meet.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: esquina

esse.etymology: Inherited from Latin ipse ('he himself, that very one'), which shifted in Iberian Romance to become the second-person/medial demonstrative ('that [near you or just mentioned]').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: esse

estalo.etymology: Deverbal noun from estalar ('to crack, snap, pop, burst'), an expressive formation imitating a sharp snapping sound (also compared with Old French estaler).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: estalo

estante.etymology: Originally the present participle of estar (< Latin stāns, stantis 'standing upright', from stāre 'to stand'), substantivized to name a standing book-rest, lectern, or shelving unit.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: estante

estar.etymology: Priberam traces estar to Latin sto, stare, with meanings concerning standing, remaining or staying firm. Modern estar also expresses location and presence, including being at a meeting. Its history does not limit it to standing upright.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: estar

estação.etymology: Learned or semi-learned descendant of Latin statiō, statiōnis ('a standing still, post, stopping place, season'), derived from stāre ('to stand').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: estação

este.etymology: Inherited from Latin iste ('that of yours'), which shifted in Vulgar Latin to become the first-person proximal demonstrative ('this [near me]').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: este

estouro.etymology: Deverbal noun from estourar ('to burst, explode, roar'), commonly traced by philologists to a Vulgar Latin *extaurāre ('to bellow or charge like a bull', from taurus 'bull') or an expressive root.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: estouro

estrada.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin (via) strāta ('paved road built of layered stone'), the feminine past participle of Classical Latin sternere ('to spread out, strew, pave').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: estrada

estragar.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin strāgāre ('to lay waste, ruin, spoil'), derived from Classical Latin strāgēs ('overthrow, devastation, wreckage', related to sternere).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: estragar

estranho.etymology: Inherited from Latin extrāneus ('external, foreign, strange, unfamiliar'), derived from extrā ('outside, beyond').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: estranho

estreia.etymology: Deverbal noun from estrear ('to use or perform for the first time, inaugurate'), derived from Old Portuguese estrea ('auspicious gift, New Year's present' < Latin strēna 'good omen, New Year's gift').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: estreia

estreito.etymology: Inherited from Latin strictus ('drawn tight, close, narrow'), past participle of stringere ('to draw tight, bind, squeeze').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: estreito

estrela.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *stēlla / *strella (Classical Latin stēlla, 'star', with intrusive -r- likely influenced by astro).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: estrela

estúdio.etymology: Borrowed from Italian studio and English studio ('artist's workroom, recording or broadcast room'), a specialized descendant of Latin studium ('zeal, study, room for study').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: estúdio

etiqueta.etymology: Borrowed from French étiquette ('attached label, price tag, court ceremonial'), from Old French estiquette ('small note stuck to a file', from estiquer 'to stick, pin' < Middle Dutch steken 'to prick, stick').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: etiqueta

eu.etymology: The subject pronoun continues Latin ego. Priberam treats it separately from same-spelled learned word-building elements. The speaker uses the ordinary personal pronoun when identifying his own department.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: eu

exatamente.etymology: Formed in Portuguese from the feminine adjective exata ('exact, accurate' < Latin exāctus) + adverbial suffix -mente.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: exatamente

exato.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin exāctus ('measured out, precise, accurate'), past participle of exigere ('to drive out, weigh, measure accurately').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: exato

experimentar.etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin expērīmentāre ('to test, put to the proof, try out'), derived from Classical Latin expērīmentum ('trial, proof, test').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: experimentar

experiência.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin experientia ('trial, proof, knowledge gained by practice'), derived from experīrī ('to try, test thoroughly').

history.meaning: to try, put to the test

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: experiência

explicar.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin explicāre ('to unfold, unroll a scroll, set forth clearly, explain'), compounded from ex- ('out') + plicāre ('to fold').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: explicar

expresso.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin expressus ('pressed out, clearly stated; in modern usage via French/English, fast direct train or pressed coffee'), past participle of exprimere ('to press out, express').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: expresso

extra.etymology: From Latin extrā ('outside, beyond, in addition to'), reinforced in modern usage as an adjective and noun by international shortening of extraordinário.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: extra

fachada.etymology: Borrowed from Italian facciata ('front wall of a building, facade'), derived from faccia ('face' < Vulgar Latin *facia, Classical faciēs).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: fachada

falante.etymology: Present participial adjective and noun of falar ('to speak, talk' < Late Latin fābulāre), denoting 'talkative, speaking' or a 'speaker (of a language or loudspeaker)'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: falante

falar.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin fābulāre (Classical deponent fābulārī 'to converse, chat, tell stories'), from fābula ('talk, story', from fārī 'to speak'), via syncope and loss of -b'- (fābulāre > fablar > falar).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: falar

falta.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fallita ('shortcoming, failure, lack'), substantivized feminine past participle of Classical Latin fallere ('to deceive, fail, be lacking').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: falta

faltar.etymology: Derived from the noun falta ('lack, absence, shortcoming' < Vulgar Latin *fallita, from Latin fallere 'to fail, be wanting') + verbal suffix -ar.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: faltar

familiar.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin familiāris ('belonging to a household, domestic, intimate, well-known'), derived from familia ('household, family').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: familiar

família.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin familia ('household establishment, kin and servants under one roof'), derived from famulus ('household servant, attendant').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: família

farmácia.etymology: Learned borrowing via Medieval Latin pharmacia from Ancient Greek pharmakeía ('preparation or use of medicines'), derived from phármakon ('medicinal herb, drug, remedy').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: farmácia

fatia.etymology: Origin uncertain in Priberam; widely connected by Iberian etymologists with Arabic fatīlah / fatīta ('crumb, piece of broken bread') or a Vulgar Latin derivative.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: fatia

favor.etymology: Borrowed from Latin favor, favōris ('goodwill, partiality, support, kindness'), derived from the verb favēre ('to be favorable to, support').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: favor

favorito.etymology: Borrowed from Italian favorito ('favored one, favorite'), past participle of favorire ('to favor', from favore < Latin favor).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: favorito

fazer.etymology: Inherited directly from Latin facere ('to make, do, perform').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: fazer

fechado.etymology: Participial adjective of fechar ('to close, shut, lock' < Vulgar Latin *pessulāre).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: fechado

fechadura.etymology: Derived in Portuguese from fechar ('to lock, close' < Vulgar Latin *pessulāre) + instrument suffix -dura, naming a door lock.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: fechadura

fechar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pessulāre ('to bolt a door'), derived from Classical Latin pessulus ('door bolt' < Ancient Greek pássalos 'peg, bolt'), with alteration of initial p- to f- (influenced by ferro or firmāre).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: fechar

feio.etymology: Inherited from Latin foedus ('foul, unseemly, ugly, deformed'), with regular Galician-Portuguese loss of intervocalic -d- (foedu > feo > feio).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: feio

feira.etymology: Priberam derives feira from Late Latin feria ('holiday, feast day'), because medieval markets gathered around church feast days—the same liturgical root that gave Portuguese its weekday names (segunda-feira to sexta-feira).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: feira

feira.notes: In Brazil, a feira (or feira livre) is the neighbourhood open-air street market.

feito.etymology: Inherited from Latin factus ('made, done'), past participle of facere ('to make, do'), with regular vocalization of preconsonantal -c- (factu > feito).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: feito

feliz.etymology: Semi-learned descendant of Latin fēlīx, fēlīcis ('fruitful, auspicious, fortunate, happy').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: feliz

feltro.etymology: Via Medieval Latin filtrum from West Germanic *filtir ('pressed, unspun wool').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: feltro

feltro.notes: In pianos, dense wool felt cushions each wooden hammer so strings ring warmly instead of clinking.

fenda.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *findita ('cleft, crack, split') or formed as a deverbal noun from fender ('to split, cleave' < Classical Latin findere).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: fenda

ferragem.etymology: Derived from ferro ('iron' < Latin ferrum) + collective suffix -agem (< Latin -āticum via Gallo-Romance), denoting ironwork or metal hardware fittings.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ferragem

ferramenta.etymology: Inherited from Latin ferrāmenta ('iron implements, tools'), originally the neuter plural of ferrāmentum ('iron tool', from ferrum 'iron'), reanalyzed in Romance as a feminine singular noun.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ferramenta

ferro.etymology: Direct continuation of Latin ferrum ('iron'), preserving Latin initial f- intact.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ferro

ferro.notes: Compare Spanish hierro, where Castilian lost initial f- and diphthongized short ĕ.

ficar.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *figicāre ('to drive in, fix firmly in place'), derived from Classical Latin fīgere ('to fasten, fix'); shifted semantically from 'being fixed in place' to 'staying, remaining, becoming'.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ficar

fila.etymology: Borrowed from French file ('row, line of persons or things one behind another'), deverbal from filer ('to spin thread in a line' < Late Latin fīlāre, from fīlum 'thread').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: fila

fim.etymology: Inherited from Latin fīnis, fīnem ('boundary, border, limit, end').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: fim

final.etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin fīnālis ('pertaining to the end, concluding, final'), derived from Classical Latin fīnis ('boundary, end').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: final

financeiro.etymology: Formed in Portuguese from finança and the ending -eiro. The adjective relates something to finance. In the office exchange, the masculine form stands for the finance department; that contextual shortening is not a claim that every use names a department.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: financeiro

fino.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fīnus ('finished to perfection, pure, slender, delicate'), back-formed from the Latin verb fīnīre ('to finish, refine').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: fino

fio.etymology: Inherited from Latin fīlum ('thread, string, filament, cutting edge of a blade'), with regular Galician-Portuguese loss of intervocalic -l- (fīlu > fio).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: fio

firme.etymology: Inherited from Latin firmus ('steadfast, stable, strong, firm').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: firme

fiscal.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin fiscālis ('pertaining to the public treasury or tax revenue'), derived from Classical Latin fiscus ('woven money-basket, public treasury').

history.meaning: of the treasury or tax inspector

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: fiscal

fita.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fīcta ('fastened band, ribbon', archaic/popular participle of fīgere 'to fasten, fix', possibly crossed with Latin vitta 'headband, fillet').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: fita

fixo.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin fīxus ('fastened, settled, stationary, fixed'), past participle of fīgere ('to drive in, fasten').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: fixo

flor.etymology: Semi-learned restoration (replacing Old Portuguese frol / chor) from Latin flōs, flōris ('flower, blossom').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: flor

floresta.etymology: From Late/Medieval Latin forestis (silva) ('unenclosed woodland outside the fenced park', from Latin forīs 'outside', via Old French forest), reshaped in Portuguese with -l- by folk-etymological association with flor ('flower').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: floresta

fogão.etymology: Formed as an augmentative of fogo ('fire', < Latin focus 'hearth, fireplace') + -ão.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: fogão

fogão.notes: Everyday word across Brazil for the kitchen cooker/stove.

folha.etymology: From Latin fŏlia, neuter plural of fŏlium ('leaf, petal, sheet') reanalysed in Late Latin as a feminine singular noun, with regular -li- > -lh-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: folha

folha.notes: Covers tree leaves, sheets of paper or sandpaper (folha de lixa), and window casements.

fome.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *faminem (for Classical Latin famēs, famem 'hunger'), with labialization of the stressed vowel before the bilabial nasal -m-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: fome

fora.etymology: Inherited from Latin forās / forīs ('out of doors, outside'), originally accusative/locative plural forms of an old noun related to foris ('door').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: fora

formal.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin fōrmālis ('pertaining to form, following established rules, official'), derived from fōrma ('shape, mold, pattern, rule').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: formal

forno.etymology: Forno continues Latin furnus ('oven, kiln'), preserving initial Latin f- intact as Portuguese regularly does (compare Spanish horno).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: forno

forno.notes: Pronounced with closed /o/ in the singular (o forno) and open /ɔ/ in the plural (os fornos).

fácil.etymology: Priberam derives fácil from Latin facilis ('easy to do'), from facere ('to do, make').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: fácil

fácil.notes: Plural fáceis drops -l and adds -is; in spoken Brazilian Portuguese fácil also functions colloquially as an adverb ('não quebra fácil').

gelo.etymology: Inherited from Latin gelum / gelu ('frost, ice').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: gelo

gelo.notes: Pronounced with closed [e] in the noun o gelo, contrasting with open [ɛ] in eu gelo ('I freeze').

giz.etymology: Priberam traces giz ultimately to Latin gypsum (from Greek gýpsos, 'chalk, plaster'), making giz an older popular doublet of learned gesso.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: giz

giz.notes: Placa de giz or escrito a giz refers to a chalk-lettered sign.

hera.etymology: From Latin hedĕra ('ivy'), through regular Portuguese loss of intervocalic -d- (hedĕra > eera > era, respelled hera after the Latin etymon).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: hera

hera.notes: Initial h- is silent in Portuguese ([ˈɛɾɐ]).

hortelã.etymology: Shortened from erva hortelã ('kitchen-garden herb'), feminine of hortelão from Late Latin hortulānus ('belonging to a garden'), built on Latin hortus ('garden').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: hortelã

hortelã.notes: Became the everyday Portuguese name for mint (Mentha).

hóspede.etymology: From Latin hospĭtem (nominative hospes, 'host, guest, traveller received under hospitality').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: hóspede

hóspede.notes: Retains proparoxytone stress on the first syllable, written with an acute accent.

infância.etymology: From Latin infantia (childhood, literally 'inability to speak').

ir.etymology: The infinitive belongs to the Latin eo, ire family for going. Modern Portuguese ir has very different-looking inflected forms, so its conjugation is not a sequence of regular changes to the written infinitive. The scene uses vou and vai.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ir

janela.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *januĕlla ('small opening, little doorway'), diminutive of Classical Latin jānua ('door, arched passage', linked to Janus, Roman god of thresholds and beginnings).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: janela

janela.notes: Distinctive to Portuguese and Galician (compare Spanish ventana < ventus 'wind', French fenêtre < fenestra).

jardim.etymology: Priberam derives jardim from French jardin. The French word has a Germanic root meaning an enclosed plot, the same family as English garden and yard. Brazilian jardim de inverno, literally winter garden, names a glassed-in sunroom.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: jardim

jornal.etymology: Priberam records jornal as a borrowing from French journal ('daily paper'), ultimately from Late Latin diurnalis ('daily', from dies, 'day').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: jornal

jornal.notes: In Brazil o jornal means both a printed newspaper and a televised news broadcast.

lente.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin lēns, lentis ('lentil'), applied in optics since the 17th century because curved glass lenses share the biconvex shape of a lentil seed.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: lente

lente.notes: Etymological twin of the inherited culinary word lentilha (< lenticŭla).

lentilha.etymology: From Latin lenticŭla ('little lentil'), diminutive of lens, lentis ('lentil'), with regular palatalization of -c'l- to -lh-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: lentilha

lentilha.notes: Optical lenses (lentes) were named after the curved shape of a lentil.

limão.etymology: Entered Iberian Romance through Andalusi Arabic laymūn, from Persian līmūn ('citrus fruit, lemon/lime').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: limão

logo.etymology: The time adverb is traced to Latin locus, meaning place. Priberam treats it separately from the modern shortening of logótipo and other same-spelled learned elements. In até logo it refers to seeing someone again soon or later, not to a visual brand mark.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: logo

lã.etymology: From Latin lāna ('wool'), showing classic Galician-Portuguese nasalization of the stressed vowel before intervocalic -n- followed by loss of -n- (lāna > lãa > lã).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: lã

lã.notes: Compare irmão (< germānum) and mão (< mănum) for the same sound change.

madeira.etymology: Inherited from Latin matĕria ('building timber, tree trunk wood, substance'), via voicing -t- > -d- and yod metathesis -ri- > -ir-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: madeira

madeira.notes: Inspired the name of the wooded Atlantic island of Madeira and pairs with learned doublet matéria.

marketing.etymology: An English loanword, explicitly identified as English by Priberam. Portuguese uses it for the business activity and field. No claim about an earlier borrowing date or an unverified ancient root is needed to explain this recorded source.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: marketing

martelo.etymology: From Late Latin martĕllus ('hammer'), diminutive of martŭlus / marcus ('hammer').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: martelo

martelo.notes: Names both a carpenter's hammer and the felt-covered wooden hammer inside a piano action.

mas.etymology: The contrasting conjunction comes from Latin magis, meaning more. Its modern use introduces a different or qualifying point. Priberam gives another entry for a same-spelled pronoun contraction; that is not the conjunction in mas valeu.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: mas

mel.etymology: Mel descends directly from Latin mel, mellis ('honey').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: mel

mel.notes: Masculine noun in Portuguese (o mel escuro), unlike feminine Spanish la miel.

melodia.etymology: Priberam traces melodia through Late Latin melodia to Greek melōidía ('singing, musical tune').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: melodia

melodia.notes: Stressed on -di- without needing a written accent under Portuguese spelling rules.

moeda.etymology: Moeda develops from Latin moneta ('mint, coin') through regular loss of intervocalic -n- between vowels in Galician-Portuguese.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: moeda

moeda.notes: Means both an individual metal coin and a country's currency.

mulher.etymology: Inherited from Latin mulĭer, muliĕris (accusative muliĕrem, 'woman, wife'), with Vulgar Latin stress shift onto -ĕ- and palatalization -li- > -lh-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: mulher

mulher.notes: Preserves open stressed [ɛ] in Brazilian and European Portuguese alike.

mãe.etymology: Priberam traces mãe (older madre) to Latin mater, matrem ('mother'), with characteristic Portuguese loss of intervocalic -tr- and nasalization.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: mãe

mãe.notes: Plural mães simply adds -s to the nasal diphthong.

mão.etymology: Inherited from Latin manus (accusative manum, 'hand'), via regular loss of intervocalic -n- and nasalization (*mão < mano < manum).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: mão

mão.notes: By extension, uma mão de tinta means 'a coat of paint' applied by hand.

nessa.etymology: A Portuguese contraction of em and essa, documented as such by Priberam. The combined written word carries both the location relation and the feminine singular demonstrative. It belongs with reunião in this sentence.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: nessa

noite.etymology: Inherited from Latin nox, noctis (accusative noctem, 'night'), showing the Western Iberian vocalization of -ct- > -it-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: noite

noite.notes: Compare leite (< lactem) and oito (< octō), vs. Spanish noche, leche, ocho.

não.etymology: The negative word continues Latin non. Priberam distinguishes the ordinary negative adverb from a noun meaning a refusal. This lesson uses negation, including its conversational repetition, rather than the countable noun.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: não

oitava.etymology: Feminine of oitavo, from Latin octāvus ('eighth', from octo 'eight'), showing the regular western Iberian vocalization of -ct- > -it- (octāva > oitava; compare noctem > noite).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: oitava

oitava.notes: Marks the eight-step diatonic span from one musical note to the next of the same name.

outono.etymology: Outono continues Latin autumnus ('autumn'), preserving the initial diphthong as ou- in Portuguese (compare Spanish otoño).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: outono

outono.notes: Used with the masculine article after em: no outono ('in autumn').

palavra.etymology: Continues Late Latin parabŏla ('comparison, proverb, spoken word'), borrowed from Greek parabolḗ, via syncope (*parabla) and consonant metathesis (*palavra).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: palavra

palavra.notes: Learned parábola was later re-borrowed for literary parables and geometric curves.

pincel.etymology: Entered via Catalan/Occitan pinzell, from Vulgar Latin *pēnicellus, reshaped from Classical Latin pēnicillus ('painter's brush').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: pincel

pires.etymology: Priberam and Houaiss trace pires to Malay piring ('small plate, saucer'), brought into Portuguese through 16th-century maritime trade in Southeast Asia.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: pires

pires.notes: Because singular o pires ends in unstressed -es, its plural is identical: os pires.

porcelana.etymology: Priberam identifies porcelana as a borrowing from Italian porcellana, originally the glossy white cowrie shell and transferred to translucent Chinese ceramics.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: porcelana

porcelana.notes: Used both for fine tableware and for traditional white ceramic electrical fuses.

pra.etymology: An informal reduced form of para. Priberam also records a Brazilian spelling pra for a contraction including the feminine article a. These are related current uses, not a claim that every spoken pra contains a separately intended article.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: pra

pra.notes: Source spelling is preserved. Informal Brazilian pra is not silently expanded in the native dialogue.

primavera.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *prīma vēra (Classical Latin prīmō vēre, 'at the start of spring'), combining prīmus ('first') and vēr ('spring').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: primavera

primavera.notes: When *verānum (> verão) shifted forward to mean 'summer', *prīma vēra took over the meaning 'spring'.

pão.etymology: Inherited from Latin pānis (accusative pānem, 'bread, loaf'), via loss of intervocalic -n- and nasalization; plural pães (< pānēs).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: pão

pão.notes: Explains why singular -ão (< -ānem) alternates with plural -ães in pão / pães and cão / cães.

quinta.etymology: Shortened from quinta-feira, from Late Latin quinta feria ('fifth liturgical day' counting from Sunday), which replaced pagan planetary names in Portuguese.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: quinta

history.meaning: fifth day of the week, Thursday

quinta.notes: Everyday speech routinely shortens quinta-feira to quinta ('na próxima quinta à tarde').

relógio.etymology: From Latin horolŏgium ('sundial, water clock'), borrowed from Greek hōrológion ('hour-indicator', from hṓra 'hour' + légein 'to tell').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: relógio

relógio.notes: Covers wall clocks, tower clocks, and wristwatches (relógio de pulso).

reunião.etymology: Priberam analyses reunião as re- plus união. The modern noun names the act of gathering or a gathering of people; a workplace meeting is one application of that meaning. The plural changes to reuniões.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: reunião

ritmo.etymology: Learned borrowing via Latin rhythmus from Greek rhythmós ('measured flow, recurring beat'), related to rheîn ('to flow').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ritmo

ritmo.notes: In Brazilian speech, an epenthetic vowel softens the -tm- cluster ([ˈʁitʃimu]).

régua.etymology: Semi-popular reflex of Latin regŭla ('straight wooden strip, ruler'), derived from regĕre ('to guide straight').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: régua

régua.notes: Portuguese split Latin regŭla into two everyday words: régua ('measuring ruler') and regra ('rule, regulation').

sabão.etymology: From Late Latin sapōnem (nominative sapo, 'soap'), an early Germanic loanword (*saipō) adopted into Latin.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sabão

sabão.notes: Regularly turned Latin -ōnem into Portuguese -ão and voiced intervocalic -p- to -b-.

ser.etymology: Priberam records Latin sedeo, -ere, meaning to sit, in the history of ser. This is not an explanation that every modern form comes regularly from a single written stem: the modern verb is irregular, including sou and é in this exchange.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: ser

sombra.etymology: Priberam traces sombra to Latin subumbra / umbra ('shade, shadow'), shared with Spanish sombra.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sombra

sombra.notes: Covers both welcome shade under a tree (na sombra) and a dark silhouette (aquela sombra).

sábado.etymology: Priberam traces sábado through Late Latin sabbatum and Greek sábbaton to Hebrew šabbāṯ ('day of rest').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: sábado

sábado.notes: With domingo, sábado is one of the two weekend days that do not use -feira in Portuguese.

tarefa.etymology: From Arabic ṭarīḥa ('piece of work assigned to be finished within a given time'), derived from ṭaraḥa ('to cast, set before').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tarefa

tarefa.notes: Portuguese preserved Arabic -f- (< pharyngeal -ḥ- adapted as labiodental -f-) where Spanish lost it (tarea).

telhado.etymology: From Latin tegulātum ('tiled roof') or formed from telha ('roof tile', < Latin tegŭla, from tegĕre 'to cover') + -ado.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: telhado

telhado.notes: Distinguished in Portuguese from o teto ('indoor ceiling', < Latin tectum).

tempestade.etymology: From Latin tempestātem (nominative tempestas, 'season, weather, storm'), derived from tempus ('time, weather condition').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tempestade

tempestade.notes: Illustrates how o tempo in Romance languages still means both 'time' and 'weather'.

tigela.etymology: Priberam derives tigela from Latin tegillum / Late Latin tegella (diminutive linked to tegere, 'to cover'), applied to a small earthenware vessel or bowl.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tigela

history.meaning: small cover; small earthen pan or bowl

tigela.notes: Standard everyday word in Brazil for a soup, cereal, or mixing bowl.

tomate.etymology: Entered Portuguese via Spanish tomate from Classical Nahuatl tomatl ('plump fruit, tomatillo').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: tomate

tomate.notes: Became a cornerstone of both Iberian and Brazilian cooking from the 16th–17th centuries onward.

valer.etymology: Valer continues Latin valeo, -ere, associated with strength, vigour or health. Its modern meanings include being worth something or being useful. The past form valeu has a conventional informal thank-you use in Brazil; here it thanks the colleague without accepting his invitation.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: valer

valsa.etymology: Priberam derives valsa from French valse, borrowed from German Walzer ('revolving three-beat dance', from walzen, 'to turn').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: valsa

valsa.notes: Feminine noun in Portuguese (a valsa, Valsa do Pátio), unlike masculine Spanish el vals.

veneziana.etymology: Priberam records veneziana as the feminine of veneziano, of or from Venice (Veneza). Slatted window shutters became so associated with Venice that the adjective turned into the everyday Brazilian noun for them.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: veneziana

verão.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *verānum [tempus] ('springtime season', derived from Classical Latin vēr, 'spring'), with regular loss of intervocalic -n- (*verānu > verão).

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: verão

verão.notes: Replaced Classical Latin aestās (preserved only in literary estio) as the everyday word for summer.

vinagre.etymology: Borrowed from Old French or Occitan vin aigre ('sour wine'), formed from Latin vīnum ('wine') + ācrem ('sharp, sour').

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: vinagre

vinagre.notes: Used both in culinary dressings and, diluted in warm water, for streak-free glass cleaning.

você.etymology: A contraction of the older address expression vossa mercê. The present word addresses another person while taking third-person verb agreement. Its history as a form of address helps explain why você vai differs from a first-person statement with vou.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: você

xícara.etymology: Priberam gives Spanish jícara as the source of xícara. The Spanish academy dictionary traces jícara to Nahuatl xicalli, a drinking vessel made from a gourd, so the Brazilian coffee cup carries a word from Mexico by way of Spanish.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: xícara
Diccionario de la lengua española (RAE): jícara

árvore.etymology: Inherited from Latin arbor, arbŏris (accusative arbŏrem, 'tree'), with lenition of post-consonantal -b- > -v-.

sources.title: Dicionário Priberam da Língua Portuguesa: árvore

árvore.notes: Kept Classical Latin's feminine gender in Portuguese (a árvore), whereas Spanish el árbol shifted to masculine.
